sentences: A large, round full moon hangs in the sky, and beneath it stand trees that have lost all their leaves.
Beyond them, a forest sinks into the mist.
The moon is bright, yet the picture is filled with the loneliness and stillness of autumn.
First, look at the writing in the upper left corner.
It says Kim Duryang painted this in mid-autumn of the gapja year.
That year was 1744, and the painter was 49 years old.
The National Museum of Korea reads this mid-autumn as the fifteenth day of the eighth lunar month, the night of Chuseok.
Kim Duryang (1696–1763) was a court painter of the Joseon dynasty.
His father, Kim Hyogang, also served the royal painting bureau, and his son and nephew followed the same path.
His art name was Namni.
He was skilled at landscapes, figures and animals alike.
In 1725 he was called to the office preparing a royal investiture, and in 1728 he painted portraits of officials honoured as meritorious subjects.
He rose to the post of byeolje in the painting bureau.
One of his pictures, a shaggy Sapsal dog, carries a poem written by King Yeongjo himself.
Now look at the moon.
As befits the Chuseok full moon, it is large and round.
A festival moon usually suggests plenty, but here, the brighter the moon, the emptier the land below seems to grow.
The trees under the moon have shed every leaf.
Their bare branches bend and reach out like the claws of a crab.
This way of drawing branches is called the crab-claw technique, a traditional method.
Critics often see the painter's confidence in these quick, unhesitating strokes.
A Korean encyclopedia describes the scene as a late autumn night, with a rushing stream in a steep valley.
The water, too, is drawn with bold, sure strokes.
In the quiet night, only the stream moves.
Look behind the trees.
There is mist, and the forest lies back beyond it.
The mist divides near trees from distant woods, giving the small picture real depth.
The picture is painted in ink with light colour on paper.
The wrinkles of the rocks and slopes are made with traditional texture strokes.
Though the literati Southern School style was spreading, he kept to the older manner here, so the work is often cited as showing his conservative side.
That does not mean he clung only to the old ways.
He is said to have learned painting from the scholar-painter Yun Duseo, and in his painting of a black dog, scholars see traces of Western methods that came by way of Qing China.
This moonlit landscape now belongs to the National Museum of Korea.
Now step back and take in the whole painting.
The round moon, the bare branches and the forest in the mist all share one sheet of paper.
For you, is the harvest full moon a moon of plenty, or a lonely one?
